note: The user-facing half of the accepted-boundaries register (id, kind, userFacingText, workaround, enforcingDiagnosticCodes). This is the ONLY home for these fields -- ledger/boundaries/*.yml keeps provenance (title, ref, codeLinkedNote) and does not repeat them. Read by `npdev why <token>`. Do not hand-edit the provenance fields back in here, and do not add these fields back to the ledger.

boundaries.userFacingText: This concept appears to have been renamed. Add a 'renamedFrom' field pointing to the original name, or rename it back.
boundaries.workaround: Declare renamedFrom by hand, pointing at the original concept/field name.

boundaries.userFacingText: Expression-valued backfills require a dry-run preview and explicit acknowledgment. Preview affected rows first via the schema migration preview endpoint.
boundaries.workaround: Call GET /api/admin/schema-migration/expression-backfill-preview, review affected rows, then acknowledge via the existing /acknowledge endpoint.

boundaries.userFacingText: FK/index checking only ever adds MISSING constraints; an extra constraint your database already has is reported as informational, never proposed for removal.
boundaries.workaround: Manage extra indexes outside NPDev; NPDev respects them and never drops them. The impact report (boot log, -ImpactOnly, and ControlPanel's schema-migration/impact endpoint) includes an advisory surplus section when there is one, but it never changes the verdict.

boundaries.userFacingText: Another app instance holds the migration lock. Wait for it to finish or clear the claim via the admin endpoint.
boundaries.workaround: The second instance waits under the real lock (a Postgres advisory lock or an H2 atomic claim row); use ControlPanel's clear() only as a deliberate manual escape hatch.

boundaries.userFacingText: This database was migrated by a newer build. Deploy a build at or after that version -- downgrade is not supported.
boundaries.workaround: Roll forward, or use mark-done deliberately after verifying by hand (or with `npdev db verify`).

boundaries.userFacingText: mark-done tells NPDev to stop trying to converge the schema and trust that you already fixed it by hand -- nothing verifies that you actually did.
boundaries.workaround: Use -ImpactOnly first to see what NPDev thinks differs, then mark done knowingly. `npdev db verify` can also check the result independently before you mark done.

boundaries.userFacingText: A refused boot can happen AFTER an earlier step already ran (e.g. an idempotent Flyway migration) -- a refusal is not guaranteed to leave the database exactly as it found it.
boundaries.workaround: Treat a refused boot as "inspect before retrying"; the schema history table records what already ran. `npdev db verify` can tell you the database's actual current state without booting.

boundaries.userFacingText: NPDev records ownership of a business table the moment its own migration creates it, before any later same-boot pass (backfill, unique-constraint tightening) can still refuse -- so a table it created can no longer end up without a record. A table that predates this (a genuinely legacy database, or one that skipped the old 'boot once with the concept present' workaround) can be adopted explicitly: GET .../ownership/preview lists which live tables would be adopted, POST .../ownership/adopt records ownership ONLY for a live table whose shape matches the model with zero difference -- never inferred, never for a table that merely shares a name. This table was not dropped because no ownership history exists is still possible, but now only for a table that genuinely was never created by this build and was never adopted.
boundaries.workaround: npdev db adopt-ownership [--apply] against a running app (preview by default, --apply to record), or boot once with the concept present the old way -- both still work.

boundaries.userFacingText: Snapshot restore can target one table, an explicit list, or every table a snapshot captured in a single call -- preflighted (nothing is written if any named table is missing live) and restored parent-before-child by foreign key order. A conflicting row (present live with different content) is still reported per table and never overwritten.
boundaries.workaround: Use the batch restore endpoint / npdev db restore --all (or --tables a,b) for more than one table; the original single-table preview/restore endpoints are unchanged for a single (snapshot, table) call.

boundaries.userFacingText: H2 to Postgres promotion copies data only. Boot against Postgres first to create the schema, then promote data.
boundaries.workaround: Call /promote/preview first, review type-mapping notes, realize the target schema by booting normally against Postgres, then call /promote/apply.

boundaries.userFacingText: H2 and MySQL commit DDL implicitly, so if a migration hook fails partway, its data changes roll back but any schema change it already made stays applied -- the database can end up in a state your model doesn't fully describe.
boundaries.workaround: Split destructive DDL and data movement into separate hooks/boots on an engine without transactional DDL (H2, MySQL). NPDev prints a warning naming the active engine before running a hook that mixes DDL with a verifySql. Postgres and SQL Server roll back fully, so the split is only needed on H2/MySQL.

boundaries.userFacingText: Each conversion hook runs in its own transaction; a later hook failing does not undo an earlier hook that already succeeded.
boundaries.workaround: Write every hook idempotent (ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS, UPDATE ... WHERE <not-yet-converted>) so it is safe to re-run after a partial failure.

boundaries.userFacingText: This conversion references a concept or field that does not exist in the pack.
boundaries.workaround: Declare a conversions[] entry (copy/split/lookup/merge/convert) instead of hand-writing convert.sql; for the uncovered case (retyping an EXISTING column in place), fall back to an operator-authored SQL hook.

boundaries.userFacingText: A destructive schema change already claimed by a conversion hook needs no separate acknowledgment token -- authoring the hook is itself the acknowledgment.
boundaries.workaround: None needed for a hook-claimed item. An unclaimed destructive item still requires the normal acknowledgment token.

boundaries.userFacingText: A forEach loop body may contain an await step, both sequentially (exactly one reachable await per iteration) and, with parallelAwait: true, in parallel across iterations (one reachable await at the loop body's top level).
boundaries.workaround: Sequential: author a forEach loop body with exactly one reachable await step. Parallel: set parallelAwait: true and put exactly one reachable await step at the loop body's top level (not nested inside a branch); other non-forEach steps may precede or follow it. A forEach nested inside a parallel forEach still needs sequential mode or a flow restructure.

boundaries.userFacingText: A field's auto-picker supports a declared filter/multi-select via field.picker; declaring the separate selectorRef property is not supported.
boundaries.workaround: Use field.picker.filter / field.picker.multiSelect directly on the reference field; the older referenceSemantics.defaultFilter grammar still works unchanged.

boundaries.userFacingText: The bootstrap Super User credential is issued (default, SUPER_USER_KEY.txt), or supplied as a hash (npdev.superuser.bootstrap-key-hash, no plaintext secret needed) or a raw key above a length floor (npdev.superuser.bootstrap-key-raw). Either way it is a short-lived handoff: claim a named administrator (POST /api/admin/superuser/claim, or `npdev admin create`) and the bootstrap credential is revoked automatically. A key that was rejected because it was already claimed/revoked is told so specifically.
boundaries.workaround: Read the issued key from SUPER_USER_KEY.txt (default), or configure npdev.superuser.bootstrap-key-hash/.bootstrap-key-raw for a deployment-supplied bootstrap credential; either way, claim a named administrator promptly and the bootstrap key stops working.

boundaries.userFacingText: Row-level write authorization's check-then-act window is closed by a real database lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction), not by a message you'd see -- a concurrent writer simply blocks.
boundaries.workaround: Nothing to do in the normal (transactional) case. In a degraded deployment with no real transaction manager wired (e.g. in-memory mode with no DataSource), this guarantee does not hold.

boundaries.userFacingText: A bandPickers entry resolves either via a named panel, or -- with no panel -- via filter/multiSelect alone, which targets the band's own collection concept directly through the same reference-lookup endpoint an FK field's picker uses. Only a picker declaring neither is refused.
boundaries.workaround: Declare filter/multiSelect (with or without a panel) on a bandPickers entry; the no-panel form needs no hand-authored Selection panel at all.

boundaries.userFacingText: Bounded contexts let one app declare multiple namespaces (contexts[]/imports[]) inside a single model and database -- but a genuinely separate service (its own deployment, its own database) still needs its own app and namespace.
boundaries.workaround: Declare contexts[]/imports[] directly (see ADR-0011 and NPDevSamples/dsl-conformance-max for a real corpus example with both isolated and non-isolated contexts). Model a separate service as its own app, not as a context.

boundaries.userFacingText: query.groupBy can join up to 3 hops across concepts (same-context or cross-context); query.where and query.aggregates still name a field on the query's own base concept only.
boundaries.workaround: Declare a join directly: groupBy: ["lote.produtoId"] (1 hop) or groupBy: ["a.b.c.d"] (3 hops, at the cap); an optional context:: prefix names the final joined concept. For a chain longer than 3 hops, use a capability-backed data source instead (listConcepts + mapList + a Java capability join) -- a path beyond the cap is refused, never silently truncated.

boundaries.userFacingText: Model changes require an app restart. Hot reload is available for metadata/UI-only changes via the admin reload endpoint, but full model changes (schema, flows) still require a restart -- the endpoint that would do a full reload is disabled by default.
boundaries.workaround: Restart the app (~30s) for a schema/logic-shaped model change; use the metadata-only fast path for a label/panel-only change (no restart needed). Full model reload can be opted into (npdev.runtime.hotswap.full-model-reload-enabled=true) but only ModelHolder.get() consumers observe the new model -- anything with a directly-injected model keeps the old one, a known split-brain risk.

boundaries.userFacingText: SQL Server has no way to express a bare 'take the last N rows' suffix -- asking for one throws rather than silently returning the wrong rows. In practice nothing in NPDev asks for it: every real call site wants 'at most N rows', which every engine can answer.
boundaries.workaround: Ask for 'at most N rows' rather than a suffix-specific row cap -- that is what every real caller in NPDev already does.

boundaries.userFacingText: A mounted plugin:java-source runs OS-process-isolated (a separate child JVM per worker, IPC dispatch) with an enforced OS-level ceiling (default 512MB memory / 50% CPU on Windows Job Objects or Linux cgroups) -- it is admission-checked at generation and boot against a bytecode denylist (filesystem/network IO, process/system control, reflection, dynamic loading, threads, scripting, detached async work, JVM internals) AND bounded at runtime. A mounted plugin:java-controller still runs in-process with the application's full privileges, admission-checked but NOT sandboxed -- memory and CPU are unbounded for that mount kind, and a hostile plugin:java-controller is not contained.
boundaries.workaround: For plugin:java-source, the OS-level ceiling is on by default; retune via npdev.runtime.plugin-ipc-pool.memory-limit-mb / .cpu-rate-percent if a real plugin's workload needs more headroom than the measured 512MB/50% default. Treat plugin:java-controller like your own application code: only mount plugins you trust there.
